name: COPD exacerbation (non-infective)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Increased breathlessness in known COPD without consolidation or fever may be a non-infective exacerbation.

redFlags: Distinguish infective trigger — may need antibiotics

harrison.pages: 2249-2259 (Chapter 303, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease); 1756 (Aspergillus/COPD exacerbation note)
clinicalPearls: An exacerbation is an episodic acute worsening of respiratory symptoms (increased dyspnea, cough, and/or change in sputum amount or character), typically evolving over less than 14 days; it may or may not be accompanied by fever, myalgias, or sore throat (p.2258).

COPD exacerbation is fundamentally a clinical diagnosis; spirometry/pulmonary function testing has not been shown to help diagnose or manage an exacerbation, in contrast to its role in asthma (p.2259).
The single strongest predictor of future exacerbations is a prior exacerbation, and the greatest single risk factor for hospitalization is a previous hospitalization for exacerbation (p.2258).

Exacerbation frequency rises as airflow obstruction worsens; patients with severe obstruction (FEV1 <50% predicted) average about 1-3 episodes per year, though some severely obstructed patients exacerbate infrequently (p.2258).

Assess both the severity of the current exacerbation and the severity of the underlying COPD, because the more severe either component, the greater the likelihood of needing hospital admission (p.2258).

Examination should focus on degree of distress, tachycardia, tachypnea, accessory muscle use, cyanosis, ability to speak in full sentences, mental status, and paradoxical abdominal wall motion (p.2258).

Blood eosinophil count (from CBC differential) is used to stratify exacerbation risk and to guide whether inhaled corticosteroids are added; counts below 100 cells/microliter derive no benefit while benefit rises above 100 and is favored above 300 (p.2255, p.2256).

Non-infective precipitants are well recognized: air pollution (including extreme-heat days), allergens, pulmonary embolism, and medication nonadherence; in a notable minority no precipitant is identified (p.2253, p.2258).
Environmental exposure and Aspergillus sensitization can drive some COPD exacerbations, relevant to the eosinophilic/allergic exacerbation phenotype (p.1756).

Cor pulmonale (overt right heart failure) is now relatively uncommon since supplemental oxygen became standard, but pulmonary hypertension should be considered in patients with persistent activity limitation or lower-extremity edema; it typically arises with FEV1 <25% predicted and chronic hypoxemia (Pao2 <55 mmHg), though some develop it from vascular destruction independent of obstruction severity (p.2252, p.2254).
harrison.pathophysiology: A range of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation and worsening respiratory symptoms. The underlying COPD substrate is fixed airflow obstruction (chronically reduced, non-normalizing FEV1/FVC) compounded by hyperinflation and air trapping; a flattened diaphragm becomes mechanically disadvantaged, raising the work of breathing during any acute decompensation. Gas exchange is impaired chiefly by ventilation-perfusion mismatching (shunt is minimal), which explains why modest supplemental oxygen usually corrects COPD hypoxemia. Hypoxemia tends not to appear until FEV1 falls below ~50% predicted, and CO2 retention is not expected until FEV1 is below ~25% predicted. Acutely, worsening obstruction and dynamic hyperinflation can precipitate alveolar hypoventilation with rising arterial CO2 and respiratory acidosis (p.2251-2252, p.2255, p.2258).
additionalDifferentials: Pneumonia (a common abnormal finding on chest imaging during a presumed exacerbation) (p.2258)
Congestive heart failure / decompensated heart failure (a frequent imaging finding and recognized comorbidity that can mimic or coexist with exacerbation) (p.2258)
Pneumothorax (asymmetric chest findings or large-airway obstruction can mimic an exacerbation) (p.2258)
Pulmonary embolism, whose incidence is increased in the setting of COPD exacerbation and should be actively considered (p.2258, p.2259)
infectionMimics: Pneumonia identified on chest x-ray or CT in a patient presenting as an exacerbation (~25% of x-rays in moderate/severe distress are abnormal, most often pneumonia) (p.2258)
nonInfectiousMimics: Congestive heart failure (frequent abnormal imaging finding mimicking exacerbation) (p.2258)
Pneumothorax (may produce chest asymmetry mimicking an exacerbation) (p.2258)
Pulmonary embolism (increased incidence during COPD exacerbations) (p.2259)
additionalInvestigations: Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as Pco2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2258)
Use of arterial pH alongside Pco2 to classify ventilatory failure (Pco2 >45 mmHg) as acute (acidemic) versus chronic, since pH changes ~0.08/10 mmHg acutely versus ~0.03/10 mmHg chronically (p.2255)
Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal findings, to detect pneumonia, heart failure, or pneumothorax (p.2258)
Consideration of investigation for pulmonary embolism given its increased incidence in exacerbations (p.2259)
Complete blood count with differential for blood eosinophil count to guide exacerbation-risk management (p.2255)

An expert-consensus objective scheme using dyspnea, vital signs, C-reactive protein, and arterial blood gases to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity (more applicable in the emergency department than outpatient setting) (p.2259)
redFlags: Respiratory acidosis with hypercarbia (Paco2 >45 mmHg and pH <=7.35) indicating acute respiratory failure and a need for ventilatory support (p.2255, p.2259)
Mental status change (confusion, sleepiness), inability to speak in complete sentences, or impaired cooperation (p.2258, p.2259)
Paradoxical abdominal wall motion, marked accessory muscle use, and central cyanosis signaling impending respiratory failure (p.2258)
Significant comorbidity such as heart failure, or an unsafe living situation, favoring inpatient management (p.2259)
New digital clubbing is NOT a feature of COPD itself and should prompt a search for another cause such as lung cancer (p.2254)
harrison.prognosis: Mechanical ventilatory support for a COPD exacerbation carries a hospital mortality of roughly 17-49%. After a hospitalization for COPD, about 20% of patients are rehospitalized within 30 days and 45% within a year, with mortality around 20% in the year following discharge. Exacerbations are also associated with greater longitudinal loss of lung function (notably in those with better baseline function) and account for the majority of COPD-related health-care expenditure (p.2253, p.2259).
pitfalls: Withholding needed supplemental oxygen for fear of CO2 retention: oxygen targeted to SpO2 88-92% is appropriate, and although it may modestly raise arterial Pco2 in some hypercarbic patients by altering ventilation-perfusion relationships, this should not deter correction of hypoxemia (p.2259).
Relying on spirometry to diagnose or manage an acute exacerbation, which is not supported by evidence (unlike in asthma) (p.2259).
Overlooking pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pneumonia, or heart failure, since each can mimic or accompany an exacerbation (p.2258, p.2259).

Attributing all exacerbations to bacterial infection: PCR-based studies show viral respiratory infections may cause more than 50% of exacerbations, and in a notable minority no specific precipitant is identifiable (p.2258).
harrison.severityClassification: Underlying COPD severity is graded by post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.7 plus FEV1 % predicted: GOLD 1 (mild) >=80%, GOLD 2 (moderate) 50-79%, GOLD 3 (severe) 30-49%, GOLD 4 (very severe) <30%. The GOLD ABE assessment further classifies patients using symptom burden (mMRC dyspnea scale or CAT score) and annual exacerbation history: groups A and B for those with 0-1 moderate exacerbations not leading to hospitalization (A = mMRC 0-1/CAT <10, B = mMRC >=2/CAT >=10), and group E for those with >=2 moderate exacerbations or >=1 leading to hospitalization. The ATS/ERS alternative grades obstruction by FEV1 z-scores rather than percent predicted. For an acute exacerbation, severity itself is a clinical determination; an expert-consensus scheme stages it using dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases (p.2255, p.2256, p.2259).
